question: In dental radiography, what is meant by 'localisation'?
options: Reducing the size of the X-ray beam so it covers only the area of interest
Establishing radiographically the position of a buried object
Identifying the cause of a fault seen on a processed radiographic film
Marking the patient's teeth before taking a radiograph
explanation: Localisation is the process of establishing radiographically the position or location of a buried object, such as an unerupted tooth.
extraWrong: Measuring the radiation dose received by the patient
Positioning the patient's head in a cephalostat
Recording where radiographs are stored in the practice

question: Which definition best describes parallax?
options: The apparent displacement of an object because of two different positions of the observer
The blurring of an image caused by the patient moving their head or jaw during the exposure
The magnification of an object that lies far from the image receptor
The overlapping of adjacent teeth caused by incorrect horizontal angulation of the beam
explanation: Parallax is the apparent displacement of an object because of two different positions of the observer: stationary objects seem to move as the point of view changes.
extraWrong: The loss of image sharpness caused by a large focal spot
The shortening of a tooth image caused by too steep a vertical angle
The fading of an image caused by exhausted processing chemicals

question: When localising an object using two radiographs taken at right angles, what does the second radiograph add?
options: The up/down dimension
The left/right dimension
The in/out dimension
The size of the object
explanation: The first radiograph locates the object in the up/down and left/right dimensions; the second locates it in the in/out dimension.
extraWrong: The age of the object
The shape of the object's roots
The density of the object

question: A plastic denture base plate containing metal markers at known points, worn by the patient during the exposure, is an example of which localisation method?
options: Vertical parallax
Horizontal parallax
Cone beam CT
A radiographic stent
explanation: A radiographic stent contains metal markers at known points, so tooth position can be measured from its relationship to the markers.
extraWrong: A dental panoramic radiograph
Two views at right angles
A bitewing radiograph

question: In the SLOB rule used for parallax localisation, what does the 'O' stand for?
options: Occlusal
Oblique
Opposite
Outer
explanation: SLOB stands for Same, Lingual, Opposite, Buccal.
extraWrong: Orthogonal
Opaque
Orthodontic

question: Using parallax, an unerupted canine seems to move in the same direction as the tubehead. Where does it lie in relation to the superimposed teeth?
options: Lingual (palatal)
Buccal (cheek side)
Mesial
Distal
explanation: Same = Lingual: if the tooth moves in the same direction as the tubehead, it is lingual (palatal) to any superimposed object.
extraWrong: Occlusal
Apical
Inferior

question: When using parallax, if an unerupted tooth seems to move in the opposite direction to the tubehead, it lies buccal to any superimposed object.
explanation: Opposite = Buccal: movement in the opposite direction to the tubehead means the tooth is buccal.

question: When using parallax, if an unerupted tooth seems to move in the same direction as the tubehead, it lies buccal to any superimposed object.
explanation: Movement in the same direction as the tubehead means the tooth is lingual (palatal); movement in the opposite direction means it is buccal.

question: Which pair of radiographs is used for horizontal parallax?
options: A dental panoramic radiograph taken from the front plus an upper standard occlusal taken from the top
Two periapicals, one centred on the upper central incisor and one on the canine region
Two bitewings, one taken on each side of the mouth
A lateral cephalogram and a dental panoramic radiograph
explanation: Horizontal parallax uses two periapicals (central incisor and canine region), or an upper standard occlusal on the midline plus a periapical or upper oblique occlusal on the canine region.
extraWrong: A periapical and a bitewing of the same region
Two dental panoramic radiographs taken a week apart
A true cephalometric lateral skull and an upper standard occlusal

question: Which pair of radiographs is used for vertical parallax?
options: Two periapicals, one centred on the central incisor and one on the canine
An upper standard occlusal and an upper oblique occlusal
A periapical and a bitewing of the same region
A dental panoramic radiograph and an upper standard occlusal
explanation: Vertical parallax uses a dental panoramic radiograph (from the front) and an upper standard occlusal (from the top).
extraWrong: Two bitewings, one taken on each side of the mouth
A lateral cephalogram and a bitewing
Two dental panoramic radiographs taken a week apart

question: For horizontal parallax, an upper standard occlusal centred on the midline can be combined with an upper oblique occlusal centred on the canine region.
explanation: Horizontal parallax can use an upper standard occlusal on the midline plus a periapical or upper oblique occlusal centred on the canine region.

question: Parallax is mainly used to assess the position of unerupted canines, odontomes and supernumeraries in which jaw?
options: The mandible
The maxilla
The temporomandibular joint
Both jaws equally
explanation: Parallax is used to assess the position of unerupted canines, odontomes and supernumeraries in the maxilla.
extraWrong: The zygomatic arch
The mandibular ramus
The hyoid bone

question: CBCT machines with a large field of view are ideal for localising unerupted or supernumerary canines in the maxilla.
explanation: CBCT machines with a small field of view (FOV) are ideal for localising unerupted or supernumerary maxillary canines.

question: Why does Cone Beam Computed Tomography (CBCT) make localisation of an unerupted tooth very easy?
options: It produces a single flat image with no superimposition of the dental arches
It uses a much lower dose than a periapical
It allows viewing of slices and moving through them in every direction
It shows the tooth at a larger magnification than plain films
explanation: CBCT lets you view slices of the patient and move back and forth, up and down, and left and right through them.
extraWrong: It needs no patient positioning at all
It produces images without using any radiation
It is quicker to take than a bitewing

question: When localising an object using two radiographs taken at right angles, what does the first radiograph locate?
options: The up/down and left/right dimensions
Only the in/out dimension
The size of the object only
The density of the object
explanation: The first radiograph locates the object in the up/down and left/right dimensions; the second locates it in the in/out dimension.
extraWrong: The vitality of the tooth
The rate of growth of the object
The colour of the object

question: For horizontal parallax using two periapicals, how is the X-ray tubehead moved between the two exposures?
options: Vertically, from below the arch to above it
It is not moved; only the receptor is moved
Horizontally across, from the central incisor to the canine region
Rotated around the back of the patient's head
explanation: Horizontal parallax uses two periapicals, one centred on the upper central incisor and one on the canine region, so the tubehead moves across horizontally.
extraWrong: Moved further away from the patient
Tilted to point upwards through the chin
Moved closer to the patient

question: Which description fits the pair of radiographs taken for vertical parallax?
options: Two from the side at different heights
Both from the top at different angles
One from each side of the face
One from the front and one from the top
explanation: Vertical parallax uses a dental panoramic radiograph (one from the front) and an upper standard occlusal (one from the top).
extraWrong: Both from the front at the same angle
One from behind and one from below
Two from the same position a week apart

question: In the SLOB rule used for parallax localisation, what does the 'L' stand for?
options: Labial
Lingual (palatal)
Lateral
Lower
explanation: SLOB stands for Same, Lingual, Opposite, Buccal: same direction as the tubehead means lingual (palatal).
extraWrong: Left
Long
Lamina

question: Which of these methods can be used to localise an unerupted tooth?
options: Taking 2 radiographs at right angles to each other
Taking a panoramic x-ray
Taking 2 radiographs lingual
Taking 2 radiographs parallel to each other
explanation: Get to see both 'side to side' and 'front to back' location of tooth.

question: Which of these methods can be used to localise an unerupted tooth?
options: 2 radiographs at right angles to each other
Taking a panoramic radiograph
Taking two lingual (palatal) radiographs
Taking 2 radiographs parallel to each other
explanation: Can see side to side & front to back.

question: When using parallax in the horizontal plane...
options: lingually positioned unerupted tooth will appear to move in opposite to tubehead
buccally positioned unerupted tooth will move in same direction to tubehead
buccally positioned unerupted tooth will appear to move in opposite to tubehead
unerupted tooth in line of arch will appear to move in opposite to tubehead
explanation: SLOB!! Same = Lingual, Buccal = Opposite.
